new_packages.label: שְׁלֵמוּת הַצַּדִּיק
new_packages.reason: These three nodes form a single independent domain: the Tzaddik's essential nature as the one who spans heaven and earth. The Rebbe explicitly declares the verse 'כִּי כֹל בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ' to be the bechina of the Tzaddik, and 'אָחֵד בִּשְׁמַיָּא וּבְאַרְעָא' as its Aramaic parallel. All three nodes — the Tzaddik's perfection, the verse, and the Aramaic gloss — are equated as three names for the same essential reality. This is the central positive domain of the Torah.

new_packages.label: מֹּחַ, בָּנִים וְתַלְמִידִים
new_packages.reason: These four nodes form the second independent domain: the transmission of the Tzaddik's mind (מֹּחַ) into the world below through sons and students. Sons and students are parallel channels of the same transmission — both are expressions of the mind remaining in the world. The two modes (abstract mind in the student; mind clothed in physical seed in the son) are parallel bechina expressions of the one act of transmission. The מֹּחַ is the dominant concept around which all others orbit. This package is the answer to the Torah's structural question: how does the Tzaddik remain 'below' after going 'above'?

new_packages.label: שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ
new_packages.label_en: Heaven and Earth — The Structural Metaphor
new_packages.reason: Heaven and earth are the structural metaphors that organize this entire Torah. They are explicitly introduced as bechinot — being above = bechina of heaven; being below = bechina of earth. They are neutral because the Torah uses them to describe persons in both positive and spiritually dangerous situations. 'מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ' (Isaiah 6) is the verse that gives meaning to the 'earth' position: even in the lowest earthly state, the divine glory is present there. The verse is a bechina-companion of 'earth' — two expressions of the positive reality of the lower realm. This neutral package provides the structural framework within which Packages 1 and 2 operate: the Tzaddik (Package 1) bridges heaven and earth (Package 3) through the transmission of mind (Package 2).

observations:
Torah LM2 #68 is a short but structurally complete teaching with no existing dataset representation (reference 1068 is entirely absent from torahData.js). Despite its brevity (12 sentences), it contains explicit bechina language forming three distinct conceptual domains:

1. PACKAGE 1 — The Tzaddik's Perfection: The core of the Torah is a direct bechina equation: the Tzaddik's completeness IS the verse 'כִּי כֹל בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ.' This is the Torah's central positive domain.

2. PACKAGE 2 — Mind, Sons and Students: The second domain concerns the transmission of the Tzaddik's mind (מֹּחַ) downward through sons and students. The Rebbe identifies מֹּחַ as 'עִקָּר' (the essential thing) and then shows that sons and students are two parallel channels of the same transmission (mind clothed in seed vs. mind in abstract form). This constitutes an independent bechina cluster — the sub-domain of what it means to 'remain below.'

3. PACKAGE 3 — Heaven and Earth: The structural metaphor (above = heaven, below = earth) is used with explicit bechina language. Heaven and earth are the neutral scaffolding within which the teaching operates.

The three packages are not cause-and-effect chains but independent thematic domains connected by eitza: the Tzaddik (Pkg 1) must use sons/students (Pkg 2) to bridge heaven and earth (Pkg 3). The teaching does not develop an explicit evil domain — the closest is the danger of the person who is 'above' and thinks they know God, when in fact they are far from Him. This is not developed into a thematic cluster but remains a structural foil to the positive teaching.

All three packages are new — none of these nodes exist in the dataset for this Torah.
